title: A Practical Comparison of Workflow Orchestration Patterns
content:
An order arrives, stock is reserved, a payment is requested, and a confirmation is sent. Drawing four connected boxes is easy. Deciding what happens when payment succeeds but the response is lost is the real workflow design problem. Compare orchestration patterns by their failure behavior before comparing their diagram editors.

Describe the work before choosing the engine

Write down the trigger, inputs, durable state, external effects, and completion condition. Separate a task from an attempt: sending a request twice may represent one business task with two execution attempts. Record which steps can safely repeat, which need a human decision, and how long work may remain unfinished.

Also distinguish the workflow's state from the business system's truth. An orchestrator can say a charge request timed out while the payment provider has already completed it. Recovery may require querying that provider and reconciling identifiers. A green execution graph alone cannot establish that all external side effects happened exactly as intended.

Pattern one: a short synchronous chain

A request handler calls steps in order and returns a result. This is a reasonable starting point for brief, bounded work where the caller needs an immediate answer. It is simple to trace because one request carries the context. It becomes awkward when steps wait for people, depend on slow systems, or must survive process restarts.

Keep the chain small and make timeout behavior explicit. If the caller gives up, decide whether the server cancels work or continues independently. Do not let a retry from the caller create a second order merely because the first response was lost. A stable business identifier and a stored result can make repeated submissions manageable.

Pattern two: queued stages and event choreography

In a queued design, an initial request durably records work and workers process it later. In choreography, components react to events without one component directing the entire sequence. Both can decouple availability, but the business journey becomes distributed across queues, consumers, databases, and logs.

Define event identifiers, message versions, duplicate handling, and a place for failed messages that require attention. Monitor age as well as count: one old item may matter more than a large temporary burst. A queue does not remove coordination work; it moves that work into delivery contracts, persistence, and reconciliation.

Use choreography when independent consumers genuinely need the same business event. Avoid making every internal function an event simply to appear decoupled. If understanding a refund requires reading five services' subscriptions, a coordinating component may make the process easier to operate.

Pattern three: a scheduled dependency graph

A directed dependency graph fits work such as extracting data, validating it, and building reports. Apache Airflow models schedules, tasks, dependencies, retries, and timeouts in its Dag documentation. That is a useful model when the central question is which bounded tasks may run after others complete.

Separate data intervals from wall-clock execution time. A rerun should know which input partition it represents rather than silently processing whatever is current. Before enabling catch-up or broad reruns, decide whether old tasks can overwrite results or resend notifications. A dependency graph describes order; task code still determines the safety of repeated effects.

Pattern four: a durable stateful workflow

A durable workflow records progress so a long-running business process can resume after worker interruption. Temporal describes workflow execution, history, and replay in its execution overview. This model is attractive for processes that wait, branch, receive external signals, or need a visible lifecycle over an extended period.

Durability introduces its own design obligations. Follow the engine's rules for deterministic orchestration code and isolate external operations in the supported task mechanism. Plan code-version compatibility for executions already in progress. A deployment may affect work that started long before the new version existed.

Provider guarantees also differ within one product. AWS documents different execution semantics for Standard, asynchronous Express, and synchronous Express workflows in its workflow-type comparison. Do not generalize an engine's “exactly once” description into a guarantee that an arbitrary remote payment will never need reconciliation.

Hypothetical example: booking a training session

Consider a hypothetical training service. Generating a preview invoice is short and has no external financial effect, so a synchronous request is adequate. Confirming a booking reserves a seat, awaits approval, and requests payment. The team models that longer process as durable state transitions rather than holding an HTTP connection open.

If payment times out, the process enters an unresolved state and checks the provider using its stable payment identifier. It does not immediately request another charge. If a seat must be released, the release is a compensating business action, not an attempt to erase history. Notifications are queued separately so an email outage does not duplicate the booking.

The design still needs an owner for unresolved bookings. Automation cannot decide every dispute from execution metadata. A human sees the booking identifier, provider status, last attempt, and safe next actions, without being shown payment secrets.

Comparison checklist for a design review

  • Which state survives a worker restart?
  • Can each externally visible effect repeat safely?
  • How are ambiguous results reconciled?
  • What happens to old executions after a code change?
  • Who handles overdue work and failed compensation?
  • Can an operator trace one business identifier across every component?

Prototype the hardest failure rather than only the happy path. Kill a worker after a durable record is written, replay an input, and simulate a remote success with a missing response. These are proposed checks, not reported test results. Choose the model whose recovery story your team can explain and maintain.
excerpt: Compare synchronous chains, queued events, dependency graphs, and durable workflows by retries, persistent state, external effects, and recovery needs.
